Case Study · World War II · 1945

The Decision to Drop
the Atomic Bomb

By the summer of 1945, Japan had lost the war. The question was how it would end and at what cost. President Harry S. Truman faced four options. Only one was chosen.

Your Investigation

Evaluate the evidence and decide: Was Truman’s decision to use the atomic bomb justified?

As you work through this case study, keep track of three questions:

  1. What did American leaders believe would happen if they did not use the bomb?
  2. What alternatives were available, and how realistic were they?
  3. Which evidence most strongly supports or challenges the decision?

Pay attention to the difference between documented facts, claims made by participants, and historians’ interpretations. The ⚡ and 🔍 badges will help you make that distinction.

~80,000 Hiroshima dead on August 6
~40,000 Nagasaki dead on August 9
~140,000 Total dead by year's end
The Options

Truman's Four Options

In the summer of 1945, President Truman and his advisors evaluated four paths to ending the war. Expand each card to read the full argument, primary source evidence, and where relevant, what we now know that Truman did not. Badges marked with a lightning bolt indicate claims revised by post-war evidence. Badges marked with a magnifier indicate genuine ongoing historical debate.

Option 01
Continue Conventional Bombing

Intensify the firebombing campaign already devastating Japanese cities. No new weapons, no invasion required.

Between March 1945 and August 1945, the U.S. firebombing campaign killed an estimated 333,000 Japanese civilians and wounded 473,000 more. The single deadliest night: March 9 to 10, 1945, when incendiary raids on Tokyo killed between 80,000 and 100,000 people in hours. By August 1945, 67 Japanese cities had been firebombed.

Truman himself acknowledged the scale: "The saturation bombing of Japan took much fiercer tolls of life than the atomic bomb." Yet Japan had not surrendered after Tokyo.

"Despite their heavy losses at Okinawa and the firebombing of Tokyo, the Japanese refused to surrender." Truman, quoted in NPS / Harry S. Truman National Historic Site

The assessment in August 1945: conventional bombing alone was not ending the war. Japanese civilian and military losses were catastrophic, but so was the determination to fight on. Planners doubted that more of the same would produce surrender before an invasion became necessary.

⚡ Fact Check: Firebombing casualties
Option 02
Ground Invasion of Japan

Land U.S. forces on the Japanese home islands via Operation Downfall, a two-phase amphibious assault beginning November 1945.

The Joint Chiefs' June 18, 1945 White House briefing laid out the planning. General Marshall compared the operation to Normandy but against a population defending home terrain. Post-war documents revealed Japan had concentrated 600,000 troops on Kyushu alone, along with thousands of suicide aircraft.

"There is reason to believe that the first 30 days in Kyushu should not exceed the price we have paid for Luzon. It is a grim fact that there is not an easy, bloodless way to victory in war." General Marshall, White House Meeting Minutes, June 18, 1945

The briefing included a casualty table from recent Pacific campaigns: Leyte 17,000 American dead. Luzon 31,000. Iwo Jima 20,000. Okinawa 34,000 ground troops plus 7,700 Navy. Operation Downfall was projected to dwarf all of these.

The Okinawa campaign, April through June 1945, was the bloodiest battle of the Pacific War. American planners used it as the closest available model for what a home-island invasion would look like.

⚡ Fact Check: The "million casualties" claim 🔍 Historians' Note
Option 03
Demonstration on Unpopulated Area

Detonate the bomb in an uninhabited location with Japanese observers present before using it on a city.

This option was advocated most forcefully by Manhattan Project scientists. The Franck Report (June 11, 1945), signed by physicists James Franck, Leo Szilard, Glenn Seaborg, and others, argued that a surprise attack on a Japanese city would destroy American moral standing and trigger a postwar arms race.

"A demonstration of the new weapon may best be made before the eyes of representatives of all United Nations, on the desert or a barren island... so that America could say: 'You see what weapon we had but did not use.'" The Franck Report, June 11, 1945

The Interim Committee discussed the idea at its May 31, 1945 meeting. The Szilard Petition (July 17, 1945), signed by 70 Manhattan Project scientists, made a similar appeal directly to Truman.

🔍 Historians' Note: Was this option seriously considered?
Option 04, The Choice Made
Drop the Bomb on an Inhabited City

Deploy atomic bombs against Japanese cities with no advance warning and no demonstration to force immediate surrender.

Target cities were chosen for specific reasons: largely undamaged by conventional bombing, primarily military-industrial, and not of exceptional cultural significance. Kyoto was removed from the list by Secretary Stimson personally.

The Potsdam Declaration (July 26, 1945) issued a final ultimatum demanding unconditional surrender. It made no mention of the atomic bomb and left the future of the Emperor deliberately vague. Japan's government rejected it publicly.

"This deliberate, premeditated destruction was our least abhorrent choice." Secretary of War Henry Stimson, Harper's Magazine, February 1947

Stimson took direct responsibility: "The ultimate responsibility for the recommendation to the President rested upon me, and I have no desire to veil it." His argument: every other available option, in his judgment, would have produced greater total loss of life. That argument remains contested by historians.

⚡ Fact Check: The Potsdam terms 🔍 Historians' Note: What ended the war? 🔍 Historians' Note: Race and the decision
The Debate

The Debate

The decision has divided historians, ethicists, and policymakers for eighty years. Below are the strongest arguments from both sides, drawn directly from primary sources.

The case for the decision
Why Truman's advisors said yes
The casualty argument

The invasion of Japan, military planners warned, would cost an enormous number of American and Japanese lives.

"My object is to save as many American lives as possible but I also have a humane feeling for the women and children of Japan." Truman to Richard Russell, August 9, 1945
⚡ Fact Check: The "million" figure
The "least abhorrent choice" argument

Stimson argued the bomb was not chosen lightly. Every other option would have caused greater total suffering.

"We had learned that such effort would require approximately 1,000,000 American casualties... This was simply an unacceptable cost." Stimson, Harper's Magazine, 1947
Japan refused to surrender

Even after the firebombing of Tokyo killed tens of thousands in a single night, Japan's military government did not surrender. The Potsdam ultimatum was publicly rejected.

🔍 Was Japan about to surrender anyway?
Truman's private moral conflict

Truman's letter to Senator Russell on August 9, written the day Nagasaki was bombed, reveals genuine moral struggle rather than celebration.

"I know that Japan is a terribly cruel and uncivilized nation in warfare but I can't bring myself to believe that, because they are beasts, we should ourselves act in the same manner." Truman to Richard Russell, August 9, 1945
The case against
Why critics said it was wrong
The moral responsibility argument

Scientists who built the bomb to stop Hitler argued that using it without warning on a city violated basic moral principles and set a catastrophic precedent.

"Such a step ought not to be made at any time without seriously considering the moral responsibilities which are involved." The Franck Report, June 11, 1945
The long-term consequences argument

The Franck Report predicted, with striking accuracy, the Cold War arms race that followed.

"The race of nuclear armaments will be on in earnest not later than the morning after our first demonstration." The Franck Report, June 11, 1945
🔍 The arms race prediction
The demonstration alternative

Scientists argued a demonstration on an unpopulated area could have achieved the same shock without mass civilian casualties. The Interim Committee dismissed this quickly but did not seriously test it.

"We respectfully petition that you exercise your power as Commander-in-Chief to rule that the United States shall not resort to the use of atomic bombs in this war unless the terms have been made public." Szilard Petition, July 17, 1945, signed by 70 Manhattan Project scientists
The racial double standard argument

Some historians argue the decision to drop the bomb on Japan rather than Germany cannot be separated from wartime anti-Japanese racism. The bomb was ready in May 1945 when Germany surrendered; it was used exclusively against an Asian nation.

🔍 Race and the bomb
What Happened

What Actually Happened

Whatever position you take on the decision, the human consequences are documented and the scale of destruction is not in question. Casualty figures are estimates with ranges of uncertainty, the destruction itself is not.

⚡ Fact Check
The "one million casualties" claim

Stimson's 1947 Harper's essay cited "approximately 1,000,000 American casualties" as the projected cost of invasion. This was a retrospective estimate written two years after the decision, not a figure drawn directly from the June 1945 military briefings. It became the standard public justification for the bomb for decades.

What the documents actually show: Historians who examined the actual June 1945 planning documents found the military's internal estimates ranged from roughly 250,000 to 500,000 American casualties for the full two-phase invasion. The million figure appears to have been inflated after the war, when the justification for the bomb was under greater scrutiny.

This does not mean the invasion would have been anything other than catastrophic. But students should treat the million-casualty figure as a post-war argument, not a pre-war fact.

Sources: Barton Bernstein, "A Postwar Myth: 500,000 U.S. Lives Saved" (1986); Rufus Miles, "Hiroshima: The Strange Myth of Half a Million American Lives Saved" (1985)
⚡ Fact Check
Conventional bombing and civilian deaths

The conventional firebombing campaign killed more people than the atomic bombs in raw numbers. The March 9 to 10, 1945 firebombing of Tokyo killed between 80,000 and 100,000 people in a single night.

Why this matters for the debate: The U.S. had already demonstrated willingness to kill tens of thousands of civilians through conventional means. The atomic bomb was qualitatively different, radiation, long-term effects, nuclear precedent, but the argument that the U.S. was uniquely restrained before the bomb does not hold up to scrutiny.

Sources: NPS Truman article; Kenneth Werrell, "Blankets of Fire" (1996)
🔍 Historians' Note
Would the invasion have been as catastrophic as claimed?

Post-war analysis revealed Japan had concentrated extraordinary forces to resist the expected invasion of Kyushu: estimates of 600,000+ troops and thousands of kamikaze aircraft are well-documented.

However, the same intercepts showing Japan's resistance preparations also showed Japan exploring surrender negotiations through the Soviet Union, a diplomatic channel the U.S. was monitoring via MAGIC decrypts.

The genuine debate: Would invasion have been catastrophic? Almost certainly yes. Would it have matched Stimson's retrospective figures? Historical evidence suggests the worst-case numbers were overstated. Whether that changes the moral verdict is a question historians continue to debate.

Sources: D.M. Giangreco, "Hell to Pay" (2009); Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, "Racing the Enemy" (2005)
🔍 Historians' Note
Was the demonstration option seriously considered?

The Interim Committee discussed the demonstration option at its May 31, 1945 meeting. Meeting minutes record the official reasoning against it: only two weapons existed, a failed detonation could strengthen Japanese resolve, and Japan might move Allied prisoners into the target area. How seriously the option was weighed is itself a matter of historical interpretation.

What historians have argued: Some scholars, including Martin Sherwin, argue the demonstration option was never given analytical attention proportionate to its moral weight, and that the scientists most committed to it were excluded from the decision-making process. Others counter that the concerns recorded in the minutes were genuine and not pretextual.

Others counter that a demonstration that failed to produce surrender would have strengthened Japan's resolve. This remains genuinely open.

Sources: The Franck Report (1945); Martin Sherwin, "A World Destroyed" (1975)
⚡ Fact Check
The Potsdam Declaration's terms and what was left out

The Potsdam Declaration demanded unconditional surrender but was deliberately vague on two points that mattered enormously to Japan's leadership: the fate of Emperor Hirohito, and the existence of the atomic bomb.

What we now know: Evidence suggests an explicit guarantee of the Emperor's position might have unlocked Japanese surrender before the bombs were dropped. When Japan did ultimately surrender, the U.S. effectively allowed the Emperor to remain anyway.

The bomb's existence was also not mentioned in the Declaration even as a warning. The Franck Report had explicitly recommended giving Japan advance knowledge. The decision not to was deliberate.

Sources: Hasegawa, "Racing the Enemy" (2005); Gar Alperovitz, "The Decision to Use the Atomic Bomb" (1995)
🔍 Historians' Note
What actually caused Japan to surrender?

For decades, the standard American narrative held that the atomic bombs caused Japan's surrender. This is what Stimson argued in 1947, and what most U.S. textbooks taught for generations.

What historians have argued: The Soviet Union declared war on Japan on August 8, the day between Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Historian Tsuyoshi Hasegawa, drawing on Japanese, Soviet, and American archives, argued in Racing the Enemy (2005) that Soviet entry was equally or more decisive than the atomic bombs, it eliminated Japan's last hope of a negotiated peace through Soviet mediation. Even Hasegawa has acknowledged that historians cannot fully separate the impact of the two shocks. The relative weight of the atomic bombings, Soviet entry, and the Emperor's personal intervention remains genuinely contested among scholars.

This is not settled history. The emperor, Japan's military leadership, the atomic bombings, and Soviet entry all belong in the analysis. The simple equation of bomb-equals-surrender that underpins the strongest pro-decision argument is more complicated than it first appears.

Sources: Hasegawa, "Racing the Enemy" (2005); Herbert Bix, "Hirohito and the Making of Modern Japan" (2000)
🔍 Historians' Note
The Franck Report's arms race prediction

The Franck Report, written in June 1945 before a single bomb had been dropped, predicted with remarkable accuracy what would happen: the Soviet Union would develop its own nuclear weapon within a few years, and an arms race would follow.

The USSR tested its first atomic bomb in August 1949, four years after Hiroshima. The Cold War nuclear arms race produced tens of thousands of warheads on both sides by the 1980s.

The scientists who signed the Franck Report anticipated the arms race with greater clarity than most political and military decision-makers. Not all Manhattan Project scientists agreed, and the report’s signatories represented one current of scientific opinion, not the whole.

Sources: The Franck Report (1945); Richard Rhodes, "The Making of the Atomic Bomb" (1986)
🔍 Historians' Note
Race, racism, and the decision

The atomic bomb program was well advanced when Germany surrendered in May 1945. The first successful full-scale test, Trinity, took place on July 16, 1945. The bomb was used exclusively against Japan, an Asian nation. Some historians argue this sequence cannot be separated from the deep anti-Japanese racism that pervaded American culture and military thinking during the war.

Wartime propaganda routinely dehumanized Japanese people in ways it did not German people. Opinion polls showed Americans were more willing to support brutal measures against Japan. Admiral Leahy, who opposed the bomb on moral grounds, raised no such objection to its use against Japan specifically.

The dominant scholarly interpretation, advanced most influentially by John Dower, holds that racism did not cause the decision, but lowered the psychological and political barriers to it. Dower's argument is that the dehumanizing racial imagery of American wartime propaganda made the targeting of Japanese civilians easier to accept than comparable action against German civilians would have been. Not all historians accept this framing, and the role of racism in the decision remains debated.

Sources: John Dower, "War Without Mercy: Race and Power in the Pacific War" (1986)
